name: Cobra Wastes
description: Cobra Wastes is a desiccated world where ancient ocean basins and dry riverbeds score the surface like the drained circulatory system of a dead body. The thin atmosphere supports only the most tenacious microbial life, which forms dark crusts on the undersides of rocks and in the shadowed depths of dry riverbeds. Vast glass plains in the southern hemisphere speak of a cataclysmic event that fused the desert sand into smooth, reflective sheets extending to the horizon, their surfaces fractured into polygonal tiles by thermal cycling.

The thin air turns the sky a pale butterscotch that deepens to burnt orange at the horizon, and the glass plains create mirages of such convincing detail that early surveyors reported cities and forests that exist nowhere on the planet. The wind raises dust devils that spiral lazily across the dead ocean basins, following the contours of riverbeds that haven't carried water in millions of years. At night the temperature drops sharply, and the glass plains contract with sounds like distant thunder, their surfaces buckling and resettling as the cold advances.

Ancient ruins dot the edges of the dry ocean basins, their architecture suggesting a civilization that existed when this world still held water. The ruins are badly eroded but retain enough structure to indicate a sophisticated society, and artifacts recovered from the sites show tool-making of high precision. An automated beacon orbits the planet, transmitting on a frequency that matches none of the known civilization's technological profile, suggesting it was placed by a different species, perhaps as a marker for what this world once was.

Cobra Wastes is a cautionary tale written in stone and sand, a world that once supported complex life and civilization and now barely sustains microbes. The ruins draw archaeologists who piece together the story of its decline, while the orbital beacon draws those who wonder who placed it and why. The glass plains suggest the cataclysm was not purely natural, and the question of whether this world was destroyed by its inhabitants or by an outside force is the central mystery that keeps researchers returning to its desolate surface.
